name: Serpiginous Choroiditis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Serpiginous Choroiditis

criteria.description: Presence of geographic areas of chorioretinal atrophy with serpiginous or creeping margins
Recurrent episodes of active choroiditis with new lesions extending from old scars
Characteristic findings on fluorescein angiography including early hypofluorescence and late hyperfluorescence of lesions
Exclusion of infectious causes such as tuberculosis and syphilis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of geographic chorioretinal atrophy with serpiginous margins and recurrent active inflammation, with exclusion of infectious causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical supported by imaging and exclusion of infectious etiologies.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Geographic chorioretinal atrophy with serpiginous margins
Progressive extension of choroidal lesions from the optic disc

laboratory: Negative infectious workup including tuberculosis and syphilis serologies
imaging: Fundus fluorescein angiography showing early hypofluorescence and late hyperfluorescence of active lesions
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) demonstrating outer retinal and RPE atrophy
Indocyanine green angiography showing hypofluorescent lesions
other: Clinical progression with geographic expansion of lesions

distinguishingFeatures: Multiple discrete choroidal lesions rather than geographic atrophy
Acute onset with multiple placoid lesions

references: Jabs DA, et al. Serpiginous choroiditis. Surv Ophthalmol. 2000;45(4): 293-320.
Kanski JJ, Bowling B. Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2015.
Bodaghi B, et al. Serpiginous choroiditis: clinical features and therapeutic options. Curr Opin Ophthalmol. 2011;22(6): 493-498.
